content: Healthy sleep is a critical aspect of childhood development, as it reflects neurological maturation through changes in sleep architecture, including sleep stage composition, quantity, and quality from infancy to adolescence. Hospitalization for acute illness introduces modifiable risk factors that can disrupt sleep, potentially impairing active brain development during illness and recovery. Therefore, it is essential to explore non-pharmacological interventions to promote sleep in hospitalized children. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of non-pharmacological sleep promotion interventions on various outcomes in hospitalized children and adolescents, including sleep quality and duration, child or parent satisfaction, cost-effectiveness, delirium incidence, length of mechanical ventilation, length of hospital stay, and mortality. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs, including cross-over trials, that investigated the effects of non-pharmacological sleep promotion interventions on children aged 1 month to 18 years in pediatric inpatient settings, such as intensive care units (ICUs) or general wards. The primary outcomes were changes in validated objective and subjective sleep measures, while secondary outcomes included child and parent satisfaction, cost-effectiveness, delirium incidence or delirium-free days, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of hospital stay, and mortality. A total of 10 trials involving 528 participants aged 3 to 22 years were included. These studies were conducted in the USA, Canada, and Brazil. Eight studies were funded by government, charity, or foundation grants, while two did not disclose funding sources. The interventions studied included behavioral approaches (e.g., massage, touch therapy, bedtime stories) and physical activity interventions. The duration and timing of these interventions varied significantly. All studies were at high risk of performance bias because participants, parents, and staff could not be blinded to group assignments. Behavioral Interventions vs. Usual Care: Five studies (145 participants) provided low-certainty evidence that multicomponent relaxation interventions did not result in clear differences in objective sleep measures compared to usual care. Individual studies found no significant differences in daytime or nighttime sleep measures, total sleep parameters, or nighttime arousals. One study (34 participants) found no effect of massage on nighttime sleep, sleep efficiency (SE), wake after sleep onset (WASO), or total sleep time (TST) in adolescents with cancer. A cross-over study in 10 children with burns suggested that touch therapy might increase TST, SE, and the number of rapid eye movement (REM) periods, but it did not affect WASO, sleep latency (SL), total REM duration, or the percentage of slow-wave sleep. Four studies (232 participants) provided very low-certainty evidence on subjective sleep measures. One study (72 participants) suggested that massage might increase sleep efficiency and reduce nighttime wakefulness over five days compared to usual care. Another study (48 participants) reported improved Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire scores after discharge in children who received a multicomponent relaxation intervention. In one study (18 participants), bedtime stories were associated with longer sleep episodes (23 minutes vs. 15 minutes) and shorter time to fall asleep (22 minutes vs. 27 minutes) compared to no story. Another study (94 participants) found that children listening to a parent-recorded story had longer sleep latency than when a parent was present, and both groups had longer sleep latency than those who listened to a stranger-recorded story or had no story with absent parents. In one study (34 participants), 87% of children reported better sleep after massage, and 92% of parents expressed a desire for their child to receive massage again. Another study (20 participants) found that parents considered music, touch, and reading components of the intervention to be acceptable, feasible, and beneficial for their children. Physical Activity Interventions vs. Usual Care: One study (29 participants) found that enhanced physical activity interventions had little to no effect on TST or SE compared to usual care (low-certainty evidence). Another study (139 participants) comparing play versus no play found inconsistent results in subjective sleep measures across different age groups. For example, TST was 49% higher in the no-play group among 4to 7-year-olds, 10% higher in 7to 11-year-olds, and 22% higher in 11to 14-year-olds. Results also varied by gender, with girls in the play group sleeping more than those in the no-play group in the younger age groups. No studies evaluated child or parent satisfaction, cost-effectiveness, delirium incidence or delirium-free days, length of mechanical ventilation, length of hospital stay, or mortality for either behavioral or physical activity interventions. Conclusions: The included studies were highly heterogeneous, preventing quantitative synthesis of the results. The narrative summary revealed inconsistent and low to very low-certainty evidence. As a result, it is unclear how non-pharmacological sleep promotion interventions affect sleep quality or duration compared to usual care or other interventions. Future research should focus on well-designed randomized trials using validated and reliable sleep assessment tools, such as polysomnography and actigraphy, to strengthen the evidence base.
